newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Expert says productivity key to Sri Lanka.
newsitem.headline: Expert says productivity key to Sri Lanka.

text.p: Sri Lanka's low productivity needs to be improved speedily if the country's goods are to be competitive in world markets and its people are to enjoy a higher living standard, a government consultant said on Friday.
"The ultimate objective (of productivity) is a high standard of living," Sunil Wijesinha, an expert on productivity who is consultant to the Ministry of Industrial Development, said in an interview.
The ministry has designated 1996-2006 the "Decade of Productivity."

One measure of living standards is per capita gross domestic product (GDP), and while Sri Lanka's is higher than its south Asian neighbours, it is relatively poor when compared to industrialised Asian countries, said Wijesinha, a fellow of the UK Institute of Management Services.
An October 18 Asia Week magazine survey puts Sri Lanka's per capita GDP at $3,415, in comparison with Malaysia ($9,470), Thailand ($7,535) and Indonesia ($3,705).
Sri Lankan economists have long decried the country's low productivity, which they say has led to high production costs, resulting in high inflation and interest rates.
Many industrialists also criticise calls to depreciate the rupee as a means of becoming competitive overseas.

Kumar Devapura, head of Tri-Star Apparel Exporters Ltd, which has 27 factories and a workforce of 24,600, recently said such calls were "an excuse made by those who cannot, or do not want to improve efficiency".
The ministry has kicked off the productivity decade by setting aside the first year for creating awareness among labour and managers.
Wijesinha said the real challenge lies in making Sri Lankan managers aware of productivity and the need for it.
He said it would be easy to convince the workforce of the benefits of improving productivity if workers could see it leads to a higher living standard.
But managers fear they would lose authority and status by joining with labour, said Wijesinha, a former chairman of Dankotuwa Porcelain Ltd, which is one of Sri Lanka's most successful export firms.
"Sri Lankan managers to whom the most disposable asset is still labour, have a long way to go to understand that work is a partnership between them and the workforce."
Local managers also have to learn that to achieve productivity, not only labour but material, energy and capital have to be managed efficiently, Wijesinha said.
The greatest fear the workforce has is that productivity leads to more work and loss of jobs, he said.
"But this fear is allayed by pointing out that countries like Japan where productivity has reached very high levels have a labour shortage, and in fact employ Sri Lankan workers."
